qualityNotes: Excellent healthcare system with high-quality hospitals, especially in major cities (Rome, Milan, Florence). English is spoken at larger hospitals but less so in smaller clinics. Public healthcare is free or low-cost for residents; tourists can access emergency care at public hospitals.
pharmacyHours: Most pharmacies open 9am-8pm. Some close for lunch (1-4pm). In large cities, some pharmacies are open 24/7. Look for the green cross sign (Croce Verde). Farmacia turns into a farmaceutico di turno (on-duty pharmacy) after hours for urgent needs.
pharmacyTips: Pharmacies are widely available. Many medications require a prescription. The pharmacist (farmacista) can advise on minor ailments. Some OTC products like ibuprofen and paracetamol are available without prescription.
prescriptionRules: EU prescriptions are accepted. Non-EU prescriptions require validation by an Italian doctor. Italy has stricter rules than some EU countries — many antibiotics and prescription medications require an Italian prescription.

restrictedMeds.name: Codeine-containing medications
restrictedMeds.note: Codeine products require a prescription in Italy. Some codeine products are restricted.

restrictedMeds.name: ADHD medications (Adderall, Ritalin, methylphenidate)
restrictedMeds.note: Controlled substances requiring an Italian prescription or special import authorization from the Ministry of Health.

restrictedMeds.name: Benzodiazepines (Valium/diazepam, Xanax/alprazolam)
restrictedMeds.note: Controlled substances. A valid prescription is required. Italy closely monitors these medications.

restrictedMeds.name: Medical cannabis
restrictedMeds.note: Medical cannabis is legal in Italy but heavily restricted to specific conditions and only available through hospital pharmacies.

bringDocumentation: Carry a doctor's letter in English/Italian listing all medications with generic names. Bring sufficient supply for your trip in original packaging. For controlled substances, carry the prescription documentation at all times. EU citizens should carry the EHIC card.

travelInsurance.requiredNote: Not legally required for short stays, but strongly recommended. EU citizens should carry EHIC/GHIC.
travelInsurance.tips: Italy's public hospitals provide emergency care free of charge to all people. For non-emergency care, you'll need travel insurance. Carry your insurance details and a 24/7 emergency contact number. Pharmacies may direct you to a hospital for serious conditions.

recommended: Hepatitis A (for extended stays or close contact with locals)
Meningococcal disease (for students or long-term stays)
vaccinations.notes: No mandatory vaccinations for travelers. Ensure routine vaccinations are up to date.

waterNotes: Tap water is safe to drink throughout Italy. In some southern regions, tap water may have a strong chlorine taste but is safe. Bottled water (acqua minerale) is widely available.
foodSafetyTips: Italy has excellent food safety. Be cautious with raw eggs (mayonnaise, tiramisu) in rural areas. Wild mushrooms (funghi) are popular — only eat those verified by a licensed mycologist. Be cautious with buffalo mozzarella from non-reputable sources. Food in restaurants and tourist areas is very safe.
medicalTourismNote: Italy is known for elective procedures, fertility treatments, and cosmetic surgery tourism, particularly in Milan and Rome.
sources: Italy Ministry of Health (Ministero della Salute)

dentalCare.availability: Good dental care throughout Italy. Private dental clinics common in cities.
dentalCare.costRange: €50-100 for consultation; €80-250 for fillings; €100-300 for extractions
dentalCare.notes: Italian dental care quality is high. Dental tourism is growing, especially in southern Italy where prices are lower. Many dentists in tourist areas speak some English.
dentalCare.emergencyTip: For dental emergencies, go to Pronto Soccorso (emergency room) at the nearest hospital. Guardia medica (after-hours medical service) can also assist.

mentalHealth.englishTherapists: English-speaking therapists available in Rome, Milan, and Florence through international practices.
mentalHealth.notes: Italy's public mental health centers (CSM) provide free services but mainly in Italian. Private therapists charge €60-120 per session.

accessibilityInfo.overview: Italy's accessibility is uneven. Modern facilities are accessible but historic cities with cobblestone streets, steps, and old buildings can be very challenging for wheelchair users.
accessibilityInfo.hospitalAccess: Modern hospitals are wheelchair accessible. Older hospital buildings may have limitations.
accessibilityInfo.transport: Major metro systems have partial elevator access. All new buses are low-floor. Trenitalia offers assistance for disabled travelers (Sala Blu service).
accessibilityInfo.tips: Book Trenitalia Sala Blu assistance 48 hours ahead. Venice is particularly challenging for wheelchairs — water buses (vaporetti) have limited access. Rome's cobblestones make manual wheelchairs difficult.

covidStatus.entryRequirements: No COVID testing or vaccination requirements for entry.
covidStatus.maskPolicy: Masks required in hospitals and healthcare facilities. No mandates elsewhere.
covidStatus.testing: Antigen tests at pharmacies (€5-15). PCR at labs (€40-60).
covidStatus.notes: Italy maintains mask rules in healthcare settings. All other COVID restrictions removed.

insuranceClaimProcess: Italian emergency rooms (Pronto Soccorso) provide emergency treatment. Non-EU visitors may receive a bill. Keep all ricevute (receipts) and referti medici (medical reports). EU citizens with TEAM (Italian EHIC) receive free emergency care. Ask for English documentation at larger hospitals.

commonCosts.note: Estimated typical out-of-pocket costs at private or international facilities. Public-system rates can be much lower (or free for residents). Actual costs vary by city, facility, and exchange rate.

medicalEvacuation.note: Local hospitals handle the vast majority of cases — air evacuation is rarely needed for tourists. If a condition exceeds local capacity: Southern European tertiary hospitals are well-equipped. Cross-border evacuation to Western Europe is reserved for highly complex cases.
